transcription_policy.shorthand: Two terminals joined by a slash, e.g. 1+/1A. Stated in Book I, PDF p7 (printed p5): 'A WIRING SHORTHAND is used to indicate connections which are to be made on the computer by simply writing the two terminal designations with a slash in between.' [verified]
transcription_policy.terminal_grammar_used_for_normalisation: Section-scoped terminals are <1-6> followed by a letter or +/-. Rotary-switch terminals are D0..D19. Matrix terminals are M1..M11 with suffix t/b, plus M10, M11, M+, M-. Auxiliary common terminals are written <1-6>com.
ocr_normalisations_applied: Letter I and lowercase l at the start of a terminal normalised to digit 1 (e.g. 'IB/1-' -> '1B/1-', 'lcom/2L' -> '1com/2L'). The grammar admits no terminal beginning with a letter except M.
Letter O inside a rotary-switch terminal normalised to digit 0 (e.g. 'DO' -> 'D0', '3G/D0').
Em dash / en dash after a section digit normalised to the minus power terminal, e.g. '1—' -> '1-'.
Every such normalisation is mechanical and reversible; where a line was NOT mechanically resolvable it is listed in per_line_flags and tagged down.

tag_meaning.verified: read by me in a rendered page image of the primary source at 500-600 dpi, or unambiguous body prose in a clean OCR layer that I cross-checked against a second printing of the same program
tag_meaning.likely: clean typeset body OCR from the primary PDF text layer, internally consistent with the terminal grammar, but not image-verified
tag_meaning.unverified: single damaged OCR line, or my inference

initial_settings: Power ON.
Place the free end of the machine's 'play' wire (the wire on M10) in 6com.
Player's 'play' wire (the wire on M11) starts free.
No slide-switch or dial pre-setting is stated.
procedure_as_printed: (Note: it will probably be most convenient to keep track of the game on a piece of paper.)
Turn power ON.
Place the free end of the machine's 'play' wire in 6 com.
Push pushbutton 6 and hold pushbutton 6 down while you push pushbutton 1. The pointer knob will turn to indicate the machine's first move.
Release both pushbuttons 1 and 6.
All succeeding moves: place the free end of the machine's 'play' wire in the BOTTOM contact of the matrix terminal corresponding to the machine's last move (as indicated by the pointer knob).
Player selects his move and indicates it by placing the free end of the player's 'play' wire in the TOP contact of the matrix terminal corresponding to his move.
Push pushbutton 6 and hold pushbutton 6 down while you push the pushbutton corresponding to the move (pushbutton 2 the second time, pushbutton 3 the third time, etc.)
Play continues until either light 1 comes on - indicating that MINIVAC wins; or light 2 comes on - indicating a tie.
To begin another game, be sure that the player's 'play' wire and the machine's 'play' wire are both free.
expected_behaviour: Light 1 ON = MINIVAC wins. [verified]
Light 2 ON = tie. [verified]
The pointer knob of the rotary switch indicates the machine's move. [verified]
The machine always moves first, and its first move is always the CENTRE of the game matrix (matrix square 9). [verified]
programs.stated_playing_rule_verbatim: The MINIVAC is so programmed that the machine will move 5 squares to the right of its own last move if and only if the human opponent has blocked that last move by moving 4 squares to the right of the machine's last move. If the human player did not move 4 squares to the right of the machine's last move, MINIVAC will move into that square and indicate a win. If the human player consistently follows the 'move 4 to the right' rule, every game will end in a tie.
programs.cannot_lose_claim_verbatim: MINIVAC can be programmed to play tic-tac-toe against a human opponent. A warning though: with this program, MINIVAC can not lose. The human opponent may tie the game, but he can never win. This is because of the decision rules which are the basis of the program.
programs.first_move_claim_verbatim: This program requires that MINIVAC make the first move; the machine's first move will always be to the center of the game matrix. A program which would allow the human opponent to move first would require more storage and processing capacity than is available on MINIVAC 601.
notes: '5 squares to the right' and '4 squares to the right' are moves around the ring of the 8 outer matrix squares (numbered 1-2-3 / 8-9-4 / 7-6-5 clockwise around centre 9 per the panel); the manual does not restate that numbering here. The ring geometry itself is NOT settled by this page - it must come from the panel photograph. [unverified as to geometry]
Matrix terminals carry a t/b suffix: Book I (PDF p27, printed p25) states 'M = matrix, 6 = terminal number (1 to 11), t = top or b for bottom ... for example M6t'. [verified]
M10 and M11 appear in this program both as wired nodes (5Y/M10, 6X/M10, 1F/M11, M9b/M11) and as the anchor points of the two free play wires.

programs.name: The Philosophic Tug of War
initial_settings: Player 1 uses pushbutton 1; player 2 uses pushbutton 6.
Pushbutton 4 is the re-set button.
procedure_as_printed: Push pushbutton 4 (re-set). Release pushbutton 4 as the rotary switch knob starts to turn.
As soon as the knob starts to turn, each player tries to control its direction using his pushbutton.
The game ends when the pointer knob stops - either at 9 (player 1 wins) or at 7 (player 2 wins).
To start another game, push the re-set button (pushbutton 4).

It turns clockwise (towards 7) if pushbuttons 1 and 6 are in different positions.

programs.name: The Mind Reading Trick
programs.book: Book VI (a re-print of the Book III 'Mind Reading Program')
programs.cross_check: The identical 32-connection set is printed independently in Book III, printed p53, PDF book2-3-4.pdf p59. initial_settings: Slide switches 4, 5 and 6 carry the three answers. LEFT = YES, RIGHT = NO.

C. Is the number odd? -> slide switch 6 LEFT for YES, RIGHT for NO
After the replies have been indicated, push pushbutton 6. The pointer knob of the rotary switch will turn to the number your friend had in mind.

programs.name: Experiment 6: The Automobile Speed Timer
procedure_as_printed: Push pushbutton 6 as a car passes the first check point (starts the timing motor).
Push pushbutton 5 as the car passes the second check point (stops the motor).
Read the speed of the passing car from the dial plate: the speed is read from the band corresponding to the LOWEST NUMBERED relay indicator light which is on.
expected_behaviour: The rotary switch runs while timing; relay indicator lights 1-5 count the revolutions.
Manual note: 'the program above indicates a revolution of the rotary switch when the dial has completed 15/16 of a revolution' - so the counted cycle is 0..15 then 15..14 then 14..13, etc.
dial_plate_calibration_as_printed: 1. Measure the distance between the two check-points.
3. Count complete revolutions per minute, multiply by 16/15.
5. Multiply by the distance in miles -> mph for one revolution.

Worked example: 50 yards = .029 miles; 45 rev/min x 16/15 = 48 rev/min; x60 = 2880 rev/hr; .029 x 2880 = 83.52 mph for one revolution; 41.76 mph for two; 27.64 mph for three (as printed - 83.52/3 = 27.84, the manual prints 27.64).

per_line_flags.note: OCR renders '2L/D 11'; the series 2L/D11, 3L/D12, 4L/D13, 5L/D14 is internally consistent.

programs.name: Experiment 7: The Train Gate Control
initial_settings: Turn power on and set the pointer knob of the rotary switch at 0.
The rotary switch at 0 represents the gate up; 7 represents the gate closed.
procedure_as_printed: 1. Push pushbutton 4.
2. While holding pushbutton 4 down, push pushbutton 5.
3. Hold pushbutton 5 down and release pushbutton 4.
4. While holding pushbutton 5 down, push pushbutton 6.
5. Hold pushbutton 6 down and release pushbutton 5.
6. Release pushbutton 6.
Then: push pushbutton 5 alone. This represents a car passing over the centre of the crossing. Notice that the gate does not close.
expected_behaviour: The gate closes (pointer knob moves to the 'gate closed' position - 7) as soon as the first switch is activated and remains closed until none of the switches is activated.
The centre switch (pushbutton 5) alone does not close the gate.

RIGHT SHIFT (divide by two): 1. Enter a binary number. 2. Beginning at the right end, set slide switch 6 to switch 5's position, 5 to 4's, and so on until switches 2-6 hold what 1-5 held. Set slide switch 1 to zero. Anything to the right of the binary point is remainder.
Leave this program wired for experiment 9.
notes: Uses matrix terminal M10 as a junction point (1U/M10, 6C/M10).

programs.name: Experiment 9: The Accumulator (multiplication by successive additions and shifts)
programs.connections: NO NEW WIRING - uses the Experiment 8 accumulator as wired.
procedure_as_printed: Worked example 6 x 10 (110 x 1010): the slide switches should all be RIGHT; push pushbuttons 4 and 5 to enter 110; output lights show 000110; record it, release the pushbuttons, enter the recorded number on the slide switches and shift left one bit -> 001100; next multiplier bit is 0, shift left again -> 011000; next multiplier bit is 1, add 110 through the pushbuttons -> 011110; record, enter on slide switches, shift left one -> 111100 (printed as '11100'); low order multiplier bit is 0, so stop.
expected_behaviour: 'The limit of this accumulator is 111111 (63).'
The printed worked example contains arithmetic slips (it writes 11100 then 111100 then '= 60' where 6 x 10 = 60 and 111100 = 60). Recorded as printed.

programs.name: Experiment 10: Division (combination shift register and subtractor)
procedure_as_printed: Worked example 27 / 5 (011011 / 101): write the dividend with a vertical line between the third and fourth digits so the divisor is greater than whatever is left of the line.
Place the dividend on the slide switches; the output lights show 011011.
Shift left one bit whenever the divisor is greater than the left-most three bits.
Subtract the divisor by entering it on pushbuttons 1, 2 and 3; place the result in the slide switches; when the subtraction proceeded properly add 1 to the low order bit.
Continue until there have been as many left shifts as there were bits to the right of the vertical line. Answer is right of the line, remainder left of it: 010 | 101 -> 27/5 = 5 remainder 2.
notes: Uses matrix terminal M10 as a junction point (3K/M10, 6F/M10).

programs.name: Experiment 11: Decimal to Binary Converter
procedure_as_printed: Enter any decimal number from 0 through 10 by turning the rotary switch to the desired position.
The binary equivalent appears in the binary output lights (light ON = 1, light OFF = 0).
notes: Heavy use of the four COMMON terminals plus 5com/6com. Note the manual's own Book I text says only FOUR common terminals exist ('The four COMMON terminals are connected together'), yet 1com through 6com are used throughout Books III-VI. NOT SETTLED by these pages - see notSettled.

programs.name: Experiment 12: Binary to Decimal Converter (tree circuit)
procedure_as_printed: Enter any binary number from 0 through 15 on slide switches 3 through 6.
Push pushbutton 6. The rotary switch will indicate the decimal equivalent of the binary number.

programs.name: Appendix: Automatic Shift Register (full six-bit)
procedure_as_printed: Enter a binary number in the shift register by pushing and releasing the appropriate pushbuttons. The number appears in the output lights.
Shift LEFT one bit by slowly turning the rotary switch dial one complete revolution.
To shift left more than one bit simply turn the dial the desired number of revolutions.

programs.name: Appendix: Two-Bit Adder with Automatic Decimal Conversion
procedure_as_printed: Enter a 2-bit binary number in slide switches 5 and 6.
Enter a second 2-bit binary number on pushbuttons 5 and 6.
The rotary switch dial will turn to the decimal sum. (Binary output lights 4, 5 and 6 will display the sum in binary.)

headline_findings_for_the_simulator: The tic-tac-toe table is 72 connections in 4 columns of 18, read column-major, on printed page 56 (PDF page 62 of book5-6.pdf). Full transcription is image-verified at 600 dpi; the only anomaly is the printed '4G/5N'.

Terminal namespaces the simulator must model: <1-6> + {A,B} (lights), {X,Y,Z} (pushbuttons), {C,E,F} (relay coil, with F/C giving the indicator lamp in series), {G,H,J,K,L,N} (relay contacts, two ganged sets: H-J/H-G and L-N/L-K), {R,S,T,U,V,W} (slide switch, LEFT = S-R and V-U, RIGHT = S-T and V-W), {+,-} (section power), plus D0-D19 (rotary, D16 = wiper, D17/D18 = motor RUN, D18/D19 = motor STOP), M1t..M9t / M1b..M9b, M10, M11, M+, M-, and 1com..6com.

M+ and M- are used in programs exactly like power terminals feeding the rotary switch and its motor (D16/M+, D18/M-, D17/M+). Whether they are physically part of the MATRIX block or a separate motor-power pair is NOT settled by the manuals.

Both pushbuttons and the rotary switch are explicitly BREAK-BEFORE-MAKE (Book I printed pp.9 and 21). A simulator that lets a normally-open contact touch the normally-closed one, even for one tick, will produce wrong behaviour in the manual's own circuits.

Relay contacts are ganged: 'The two relay arms are connected together mechanically with a plastic crossbar. Both arms move together and make or break contact at the same time.' Relays can also be actuated MANUALLY - several programs require the operator to push relays left before play (Electronic Maze short path; Farmer/Goose/Corn/Wolf reset; Full Adder carry-in).

The motor is a real DC motor with a friction drive and current-limiting resistors: RUN = power across D17/D18, STOP = a short across D18/D19, and reversing the polarity across D17/D18 reverses rotation (Book I Experiment 14). Timing-dependent programs (metronome, traffic light, speed timer, radar) depend on continuous rotation, so the simulator needs a modelled dial speed.

Programs routinely make more than two connections to one terminal - the manuals say every terminal has two holes, and the com terminals have four - so the simulator's netlist must allow multi-way joins per terminal, with a documented limit.

Four Book V/VI programs use a free-ended 'play wire' the operator touches to a terminal rather than plugs in (Tic-Tac-Toe M10/M11, Electronic Maze M+, Arabic Numeral Recognition four wires each on M10 and M11, Maze Solver 6E). The simulator needs a first-class 'touch a terminal with a loose wire end' input.
Book VI's three sequence games share one 38-connection 'basic sequence recognition circuit'; getting that one subcircuit right buys the Secret Code, Combination Lock and Electronic Maze at once.

The Book I experiments 1-14 are all short (2-10 wires) and every one of them has a stated observable; they are the right conformance-suite floor and all fourteen are transcribed here, ten of them image-verified.
The Book I answer pages (printed 29-32) contain 20 more small programs but are hand-lettered; their OCR is degraded and they are all tagged [unverified]. They need a 500 dpi image pass before use.
not_settled_by_the_sources: How many COMMON terminals there physically are. Book I printed p25 says four; Books III-VI address six (1com..6com). Needs the panel photograph.
Where M+ and M- physically sit on the panel, and whether they are matrix terminals, motor-power terminals, or main supply terminals. The manuals only use them in wiring lists.

The ring order of the nine matrix squares that makes the tic-tac-toe 'move 4/5 squares to the right' rule concrete. Book VI states the rule but never restates the numbering; Book I only gives the naming convention M<n><t|b>.

Whether the six section minus terminals (1- .. 6-) and plus terminals are one common supply rail or six separately-fused nodes. Book I Exp 12 vs Exp 13 print 6-/D18 and 5-/D18 for the same circuit, which implies one rail, but no page says so.
The character code table for Experiment 12 (Arabic Numeral Recognition), printed p22. The OCR of the FORM/CODE table is unreadable and it was not image-verified.
Whether Book I Experiment 12's '6-/D18' or Experiment 13's '5-/D18' is the typo (or whether both are correct because the rails are common).
Whether the Combination Lock's '5A/6J' or the other two printings' '6A/6J' is the typo in the basic sequence recognition circuit.

The exact rotary-switch dial speed and the friction-drive behaviour, which every timing program depends on. Book I says only that the resistors limit motor current; no rpm figure is given (Book V asks the reader to count revolutions per minute on their own machine).
Book I answer pages 29-32 (PDF pages 31-34): all 20 answer programs need a 500 dpi image read. I ran out of image budget after eleven reads.

Book V Experiment 19's '4H/5U' and Experiment 14's '4F/5G', and the Super Circuit's '4C/3-' and '5H/4-': each is a single line whose terminal class is out of pattern for its program. Each needs a single-line image read.
